description: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection. Early recognition and treatment (antibiotics within 1 hour, fluid resuscitation) dramatically improves survival.

decision_rules.description: Sepsis with hypotension requiring vasopressors and lactate > 2 mmol/L

criteria.name: Hypotension despite fluids
criteria.definition: MAP < 65 mmHg after fluid challenge, requiring vasopressors

action.procedure: Sepsis bundle: IV access, fluids, vasopressors, antibiotics
action.rationale: Septic shock mortality 40-60%, each hour delay in antibiotics increases mortality 7.6%

decision_rules.evidence_text: Septic shock is defined by sepsis with persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP >= 65 and serum lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation. Mortality 40-60%.

decision_rules.description: Quick SOFA score >= 2 indicates high risk of poor outcome
decision_rules.evidence_text: qSOFA (quick SOFA): Altered mental status (1 pt), RR >= 22 (1 pt), SBP <= 100 (1 pt). Score >= 2 indicates high risk of poor outcome and should trigger further evaluation for organ dysfunction.

decision_rules.description: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome with suspected infection

action.rationale: SIRS with infection source requires evaluation for sepsis

decision_rules.evidence_text: SIRS criteria: Temp > 38C or < 36C, HR > 90, RR > 20 or PaCO2 < 32, WBC > 12K or < 4K or > 10% bands. >= 2 criteria with suspected infection = sepsis.

decision_rules.description: Urinary tract infection with systemic signs

action.rationale: Urosepsis common source, requires prompt antibiotics

decision_rules.evidence_text: Urinary tract is most common source of sepsis (25-30%). Elderly and immunocompromised may have atypical presentations. Prompt source control and antibiotics essential.

action.rationale: Pneumonia is second most common sepsis source

decision_rules.evidence_text: Pneumonia accounts for ~20% of sepsis cases. CURB-65 or PSI can help stratify severity. Severe CAP with sepsis criteria requires ICU admission.

action.rationale: Abdominal sepsis often requires surgical source control

decision_rules.evidence_text: Intra-abdominal sepsis has mortality 20-60% depending on source control. Perforated viscus, abscess, and biliary sepsis require urgent surgical consultation.

text_chunks.title: Sepsis Definition and Recognition
text_chunks.content: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection. Sepsis-3 defines it as suspected infection + SOFA score increase >= 2. qSOFA (quick SOFA) is a bedside screening tool: Altered mental status (GCS < 15), Respiratory rate >= 22, Systolic BP <= 100 mmHg. Score >= 2 indicates high risk. Traditional SIRS criteria (temp, HR, RR, WBC) are sensitive but less specific for sepsis.

text_chunks.title: Sepsis Bundle - Hour 1
text_chunks.content: Hour-1 Bundle for Sepsis: (1) Measure lactate, remeasure if initial lactate > 2 mmol/L. (2) Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics. (3) Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics - target within 1 hour of recognition. (4) Begin rapid IV fluid resuscitation - 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >= 4. (5) Apply vasopressors if hypotensive during or after fluid resuscitation to maintain MAP >= 65 mmHg. Early aggressive care reduces mortality significantly.

text_chunks.title: Sepsis Red Flags
text_chunks.content: Red flags requiring immediate sepsis workup: (1) Fever with confusion/altered mental status, (2) Rigors with hypotension, (3) Fever with tachycardia and tachypnea, (4) Known immunosuppression with any infection signs, (5) Recent instrumentation (catheter, surgery) with fever, (6) Petechiae or purpura with fever (consider meningococcemia), (7) Elderly with vague decline and low-grade fever, (8) Diabetic with infection and hyperglycemia.

text_chunks.title: Sepsis Epidemiology
text_chunks.content: Sepsis affects >1.7 million adults in US annually with >270,000 deaths. Hospital mortality 15-30%, higher in septic shock (40-60%). Most common sources: respiratory (35-50%), genitourinary (20-30%), abdominal (15-20%), skin/soft tissue (5-10%). Risk factors: age > 65, immunosuppression, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, cancer, recent hospitalization. Every hour delay in antibiotics increases mortality by 7.6%.
